questions.stem: An unknown element conducts electricity well and its oxide neutralises dilute acid. How should it be classified?

options.text: Metal, because both tests point that way
options.explanation: Good conductivity and a basic oxide are the two metal markers together.

options.text: Non-metal, because some non-metals conduct too
options.explanation: Graphite is the famous conducting exception, but the basic oxide here confirms the metal verdict.

options.text: Metalloid, since anything that conducts sits on the border line
options.explanation: Border position, not conductivity, is what names a semi-metal.

options.text: Cannot be classified without its melting point
options.explanation: The two spec tests are sufficient; melting point is supporting evidence only.

questions.stem: An element is dull and brittle, and its oxide dissolves in water to give an acidic solution. Which class fits?

options.text: Non-metal
options.explanation: Dull, brittle traits and an acidic oxide are the standard non-metal markers.

options.text: Metal, because all solid elements are metals
options.explanation: Several non-metals are solid, including sulfur and iodine; state alone never classifies.

options.text: Metalloid, because acidity always signals a border element
options.explanation: Acidic oxides are the ordinary non-metal signature; only table position names a metalloid.
options.misconception: oxide acidity misread as metalloid marker

questions.stem: Which comparison row between metals and non-metals is correct?

options.text: Outer-shell electrons: metals hold one to three, non-metals four to seven
options.explanation: This matches the electron-arrangement comparison drawn in the note.

options.text: Outer-shell electrons: metals hold four to seven, non-metals one to three
options.explanation: The counts are reversed; metals hold the smaller number of outer electrons.

options.text: Bonding: metals share electrons, non-metals lose them
options.explanation: It runs the other way: metal atoms lose electrons to bond, non-metals share.

options.text: Melting points: metals low, non-metals high
options.explanation: Metals generally melt at high temperatures and non-metals at low ones.

questions.stem: A solid element is lustrous and can be bent into shape, but a classmate calls it a non-metal because it is solid. What is the soundest reply?

options.text: It is a metal: malleability and a lustrous look outweigh state, which varies among non-metals too
options.explanation: The physical character is diagnostic here, and several non-metals are solid anyway.

options.text: Agree with the classmate: every solid is a non-metal
options.explanation: Most solid elements are metals, so state alone points the wrong way.

options.text: Agree, because metals can never be bent into shape
options.explanation: Malleability is one of the classic metal properties listed in the note.

options.text: Call it a metalloid because the class is disputed
options.explanation: A classmate's error does not create border status; the tests still say metal.

questions.stem: Why do conductivity and oxide character work together as a classification pair?

options.text: Both reflect the same underlying outer-shell electron count, so the two verdicts normally agree
options.explanation: One test probes charge flow and the other bonding behaviour, and both trace back to how many outer electrons the element holds.

options.text: They test unrelated properties, so using both wastes time
options.explanation: They are two windows on one cause, which is exactly why agreement is convincing.

options.text: Conductivity alone decides, and the oxide test merely checks practical skills
options.explanation: Each test can mislead on its own; graphite is the classic conductivity exception.

questions.stem: State the acid-base character of metal oxides.
State how many outer-shell electrons a non-metal atom holds.
questions.modelAnswer: Four to seven (metals hold one to three).

questions.stem: Explain why the electrical conductivity test is decisive when sorting metals from non-metals.
questions.modelAnswer: Because metals conduct well while non-metals are poor conductors, so a conductivity reading separates the two classes cleanly.

questions.stem: The oxide of element X dissolves in water and the solution turns universal indicator purple, well above pH 7. State the acid-base character of X's oxide and the class of element X.
questions.modelAnswer: The oxide is basic (alkaline), so X is a metal — metal oxides are basic.

questions.stem: An element sits immediately to the left of the zig-zag line on the periodic table. Classify it.

options.text: Metal, because the metals occupy the left of the table
options.explanation: Position to the left of the dividing line is the metal side of the table.

options.text: Non-metal, because everything near the line is a non-metal
options.explanation: Non-metals sit on the right; the immediate neighbourhood on the left is metallic.

options.text: Semi-metal, because every element near the line is one
options.explanation: Only elements that touch the line take the semi-metal label.

questions.stem: Which statement about how the two classes share the periodic table is true?

options.text: Metals make up the vast majority of elements
options.explanation: Colouring the classes on a full table shows the metal region dominating the chart.

options.text: The two classes split the table roughly half and half
options.explanation: The metal region is far larger, so the split is nowhere near even.

options.text: Non-metals occupy most of the middle rows
options.explanation: The middle of the table is metallic; non-metals crowd the right-hand edge.

questions.stem: What does the zig-zag line on the periodic table mark?

options.text: The division between the metal region on the left and the non-metal region on the right
options.explanation: That dividing role is exactly why the line is drawn.

options.text: The boundary between periods and groups
options.explanation: Periods and groups are table scaffolding, not the class divide.

options.text: The edge of the transition-metals block only
options.explanation: The line runs the height of the table separating both classes, not one block.

questions.stem: An element borders the zig-zag line and shows a mix of metallic and non-metallic traits. Which term applies, and why is it used?

options.text: Semi-metal or metalloid, because such elements resist clean classification
options.explanation: The special term exists precisely for elements with characteristics of both sides.

options.text: Transition metal, because border elements belong to the central block
options.explanation: Transition metals sit inside the metal region and show no such mixed character.

options.text: Noble gas, because border elements are unreactive
options.explanation: Noble gases form the far-right group; nothing about the border implies low reactivity.

options.text: Alloy, because border elements mix both behaviours
options.explanation: An alloy is a mixture of metals, not a class assigned to a single element.
options.misconception: class term confused with mixture term

questions.stem: With no property data at all, how do you classify an element shown only as a symbol on the table?

options.text: Read its position against the zig-zag line: left names it a metal, right a non-metal
options.explanation: Position is the designed classifier for this spec point.

options.text: Learn each element's class individually from a full list
options.explanation: The table's own geography does the work, so no list is needed.

options.text: Assume every element with a one-letter symbol is a metal
options.explanation: Symbol length says nothing about class; hydrogen sits on the left yet is a non-metal.

questions.stem: State which side of the periodic table the non-metals occupy.
questions.modelAnswer: The right-hand side — metals sit on the left.

questions.stem: State which class of element makes up the vast majority of the periodic table.
Explain why elements bordering the zig-zag line are hard to classify as simply metal or non-metal.
questions.modelAnswer: Because elements bordering that line show traits of both sides — they are the semi-metals, or metalloids.

questions.stem: A newly discovered element is placed three columns in from the right-hand edge of the periodic table, clear of the zig-zag line. State its class using its position alone.
questions.modelAnswer: A non-metal — on the periodic table metals sit on the left and non-metals on the right, so position is itself the classifier.
